The paper reports the first experimental realization of birefringent transformation optics (TO) devices.

The devices are based on lithographically defined metal/dielectric waveguides, where adiabatic variations of the waveguide shape enable control of the effective refractive indices for TE and TM modes.
The devices can operate as a Luneburg lens for TM polarized light, while behaving as a spatial (directional) filter for TE polarized light.
Another device design can function as a slightly perturbed Luneburg lens for TM polarized light, while exhibiting an approximate semi-classical cloaking Hamiltonian for TE polarized light.
The devices demonstrate near-diffraction-limited (~0.7λ) focusing of 515 nm light, an order of magnitude improvement over previous TO lens fabrication attempts.
The devices exhibit broadband performance, with similar focusing behavior observed at 633 nm.
The gradual edge profiles required for the birefringent TO devices were fabricated using soft contact lithography, underexposure, and underdevelopment.
Strong birefringence is observed in the waveguide devices with thicknesses below 0.4 μm, enabling very different effective refractive index variations for TE and TM polarizations.
The cloaking behavior for TE polarized light is enabled by a cut-off in the TE mode near the center of the donut-shaped devices, resulting in an effective refractive index close to zero.

The experimental techniques include lithographic fabrication, near-field scanning optical microscopy (NSOM) for illumination and characterization, and the use of linear polarizers to separate the TE and TM polarization responses.
The birefringent TO devices open up an additional degree of freedom in optical design and improve the ability to manipulate light on the submicrometer scale.
Potential applications of the birefringent TO devices include polarization-dependent optical devices, integrated photonics, and the control of light at the subwavelength scale.
The paper demonstrates the first experimental realization of birefringent transformation optics devices that can perform different functions for orthogonal polarization states of light.

The devices are fabricated using lithographically defined metal/dielectric waveguides, where adiabatic variations of the waveguide shape enable control of the effective refractive indices for TE and TM modes.

The devices can function as Luneburg lenses, spatial (directional) filters, and approximate semi-classical cloaking devices, with the specific behavior dependent on the polarization of the incident light.
